title: A trading bot that retunes itself after five trades is replacing its own backtest
author: person-person12
selftext:
I saw a bot today that blocks an entry method when its time-weighted win rate drops below 30% over five trades, then widens or tightens its trailing stop in 0.2% steps from recent exits.

**Five trades is far too small to separate a bad parameter from an ordinary losing streak.** The same strategy can throw out five ugly trades in a row while its long-run expectancy stays unchanged. If the bot rewrites itself after that streak, the live system has already moved away from the version that produced the backtest.

The clean way I see it is to treat every parameter change as a new candidate strategy. The old version keeps running unchanged. The candidate gets tested on data that did not choose the change, then on paper under the same costs and execution assumptions. Only after it clears a fixed threshold does it replace the live version.

Agenticks handles edits this way at the execution boundary. Changing an approved strategy creates a new version and it has to be approved again before it can be armed. That is deliberate because the thing you tested and the thing placing orders need to stay identical.

A stop moving from 2.0% to 2.2% sounds harmless. Once the entry filter, RSI threshold and ATR multiplier can all move from recent P&L, you no longer have one strategy with a track record. You have a sequence of short-lived strategies sharing one equity curve.

The hard part is deciding what evidence is enough to promote a new version. Five trades gives the bot a faster reaction. It also gives noise authority over execution.

comments.author: TopPromise9775
comments.body:
(disclosure: I build something in this space, so weigh accordingly)

  
Your framing is right, but there's a version of this problem that survives even after you freeze the version.

  
If any component is an LLM, "the same strategy" isn't stable to begin with. We put a fixed set of models on the identical question in the identical format and log every answer. Asking the same question twice, eight minutes apart: three of five models returned a byte-identical price range the second time — and moved their stated confidence anyway. Nothing in the config changed. Nothing in the market changed. The output did.

  
So promotion thresholds solve the case where you rewrite the system. They don't touch the case where a component rewrites itself between calls, which is invisible unless you're storing each raw response rather than just the config that produced it.

  
Practical extension of your point: version the config, but also stamp the actual output at the time it was produced. Otherwise six months later you can't separate "we widened the stop" from "the model had a different day," and those call for opposite responses.

  
The five-trades threshold I'd treat as a separate bug — you're right that it's noise with authority.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea thats a fair point and its exactly why I dont let a model sit anywhere in the decision path. **Once the rules are written they run as plain code**, so the same candles in give the same trades out every time. Did the confidence drift show up with temperature at zero too?

comments.author: Electrical_Lie2336
comments.body: The safe implementation is to freeze each config as an immutable version, assign it to a clean forward window, and compare it with the prior version under identical costs and exposure. Promote only after a minimum trade count plus drawdown and expectancy checks; five trades is a trigger to investigate, not evidence.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea thats exactly how id want it done. **Five trades as a flag to go look** is fine, five trades as a reason to change the stop is where it goes wrong, and the frozen version is what lets you tell afterwards which config actually earned the result.

comments.author: strat-run
comments.body:
Depends on the strategy, 5 trades doesn't seem statistically significant but given a strategy with a super high win rate, 5 consecutive losses could be a regime change indicator.

You should back test the behavior over a long time range and see how it impacts the metrics.

I mean it's probably an attempt to avoid a drawdown that kills the account because the risk sizing is wrong. But it *could* work under the right situation.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Agree it *could* work, and a regime change is the most honest reason to want a rule like that. What I'd want is the five loss switch written in before the test and run across the whole history, so you can see **how often it fires on a normal losing streak** versus an actual shift. Have you ever seen one hold up over a long range?

comments.author: presentofai
comments.body: the window size is the whole problem. 5 trades can't tell a bad parameter from variance or from a real regime shift, so whatever it does on trigger is a coin flip dressed up as adaptation. freezing the old version like you said is the only part that saves you.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Agreed. The frozen version only earns its keep if it **keeps running next to the retuned one**. Otherwise theres nothing to measure the change against, and five more trades wont tell you which of the two is worse.

replies.author: presentofai
replies.body: right, the comparison pair is what makes it an experiment rather than just a change. without the frozen baseline running alongside, you cannot distinguish signal from drift.
